title: Thiebou Diola, the Casamance ‘C’est Bon’
author: Dumplings And More
desc: Grilled sea bream and prawns on rice fried with dried toufa, yokhos and shrimp, topped with a pepper-onion marinade and a crushed okra-and-bissap-leaf beugueuthie.
longDesc: The page attributes this dish explicitly to the Diola community of Casamance. A sea bream marinates in lemon, garlic, green chile, pepper and mustard and is grilled, pan-cooked or oven-cooked until nicely browned. Cooked rice is fried with 50 g each of toufa and yokhos (dried seafood) and small shrimp. An onion sauce cooks a few minutes with lime; a raw pepper-and-onion marinade rests 30 minutes; okra boils 10 minutes and green bissap leaves 5, crushed together into the beugueuthie. Prawns are pan-cooked. Everything is stacked on the rice and served with lime and, optionally, palm oil.
ingredients: 50 g small dried or fresh shrimp
Salt, pepper, peanut oil — quantities not printed
equipment: Pot for the okra and bissap leaves
steps: Mix the lemon juice, garlic, green chile, pepper and mustard for the fish marinade.
Brush the sea bream with the marinade, cover and rest 30 minutes (the page header says 1 hour of marinating; the method says 30 — both are recorded).
Cook the fish over coals, in a pan or in the oven with a drizzle of peanut oil, until nicely browned. No time or temperature is printed.
Fry the cooked rice with the toufa, yokhos and small shrimp. Add salt if needed and keep warm.
Sauté the onion in a little oil, add the green pepper, chile, parsley, garlic, salt and pepper. Cook a few minutes, add the lime juice and let it reduce slightly. Set aside.
Mix the peppers, onions, salt, mustard and lime juice and marinate 30 minutes.
Boil the okra in salted water 10 minutes and drain.
Boil the green bissap 5 minutes, drain and salt. Chop or coarsely crush it with the okra to make the beugueuthie.
Cook the prawns in a pan with a little peanut oil, salt and pepper.
Spread the rice on a large dish. Top with the onion and pepper marinade, the beugueuthie, the okra, the prawns and the grilled fish.
Serve with lime and, if wanted, palm oil.
chefTips: ‘Nicely browned’ is the one fish cue; no time is printed for the fish or the prawns.
Toufa and yokhos are bought, dried and called ‘lightly fermented’ by the page, which gives no process for them; small dried shrimp, smoked fish or shrimp powder are the printed substitutes.
Fry the dried seafood with the rice, not in the sauce.
Beugueuthie is the bissap-leaf and okra mash; the page also gives ‘beugueudj’ as a Casamance name for bissap sauce elsewhere.
commonMistakes: Cooking the prawns without a cue.
reheating: Reheat the rice in a pan; serve the marinade and beugueuthie cold.
healthBenefits: Fish and prawns provide lean protein and omega-3.
Okra and bissap leaves add fibre and vitamin C.
culturalNote: ‘Thiebou diola is specific to the Diola community of Casamance, which is one of the Senegalese ethnic groups,’ says the page — the only entry in this collection in which a source explicitly attributes a dish to the Jola/Diola. The attribution is the source’s own. The page adds that the dish is less known than ceebu jen.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Thiebou Diola: The Senegalese C’est bon from Casamance’. BYLINE: ‘dumplingsandmore’ (Dumplings And More) — a site-name byline, flagged. DATE: NOT PRINTED; metadata shows a last-updated 2026-06-12. It survives the sourcing bar only because it has a byline — marginal, flagged. Yield: Serves 4. Prep 30 min, cooking 1 h, marinating 1 h, total 2 h. SINGLE-PASS.
DISCREPANCY: the header gives 1 hour of marinating; the method says rest the fish 30 minutes. Both reported.

FERMENTATION RULE: toufa and yokhos are described as dried seafood ‘lightly fermented’, but the page gives no fermentation step, no soaking or rinsing, no time and no cue. They are fried directly with the cooked rice. This is the weakest fermented-ingredient documentation in the collection. The page does not mention guedj, yeet or nététou.

ATTRIBUTION as the source states it: ‘Thiebou diola is specific to the Diola community of Casamance, which is one of the Senegalese ethnic groups.’ Casamance is called ‘a fertile, green region open to the Atlantic’.
ABSENT, not estimated: cooking times for the fish and prawns, quantities of salt, pepper, oil in several components.
